podcast.title: The Beatles' Final Public Performance Venue (1969)
podcast.body: The rooftop of the Apple Records building in London served as the unexpected stage for The Beatles' last public performance together on January 30, 1969. "el 30 de enero de 1969 en la zoteada de Apple Records tocarían juntos por última vez los Beatles."

podcast.title: Stock Price Surge (2001-2007)
podcast.body: Before the iTunes music player was revealed on January 1, 2001, Apple's stock price was 39 cents. It remained around 39 cents in 2002 and dropped to 32 cents in 2003 when the iTunes music store went online. However, by 2004, it rose to 116 cents, then 254 cents in 2005, 297 cents by the end of 2006, and 597 cents a year later. The iPod and iTunes ecosystem saved both the music industry and Apple itself, which at one point controlled 70% of all digital music sales worldwide. Today, Apple boasts a market cap of approximately $3.5 trillion. "A January 1st, 2001, about 10 days before the iTunes music player was revealed, Apple stock price was just 39 cents."

podcast.title: iPod Introduction (2001)
podcast.body: On October 23, 2001, Steve Jobs unveiled the iPod at an Apple event, famously marketing it with the slogan "a thousand songs in your pocket." This device, initially exclusive to Mac users but later expanding to Windows, utilized iTunes Music Player and rapidly became a cornerstone of digital music consumption, often loaded with MP3s. "Steve Jobs introduced it at an Apple event on October 23, 2001."

podcast.title: iPod Introduction and Initial Capacity (2001)
podcast.body: The iPod was officially introduced to the world on October 23rd, 2001. The inaugural model featured a five-gigabyte hard drive, which was capable of storing approximately one thousand songs. "Anyway, the iPod was introduced to the world on October 23rd, 2001. It had a five gig hard drive and that was good for, well, about a thousand songs."

podcast.title: iTunes Music Store Windows Compatibility (2002)
podcast.body: The iPod's market dominance was significantly bolstered after the iTunes Music Store was made compatible with Windows computers in July 2002. This expansion broadened Apple's ecosystem to a much larger user base, making the iPod even more accessible. "The iPod changed everything about portable music, especially after the iTunes music star was made compatible with Windows computers in July 2002."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: iTunes Music Store and iPod Launch (2003)
podcast.body: Apple, under Steve Jobs, emerged as the savior of the recorded music industry by introducing the iTunes music store in April 2003 (initially Mac-only, then Windows in October). This followed the earlier release of the iTunes media player and the iPod, which was marketed as holding "a thousand songs in your pocket." Jobs convinced the five major record labels in 2002 to license their music, selling songs for 99 cents with Apple taking 30%. This move changed everything, leading to the iPod becoming the fastest-selling consumer electronic product and providing the first effective solution to music piracy by offering legal, clean digital tracks. "the iTunes music store was introduced in April 2003."

podcast.title: First iPhone Commercial (2007)
podcast.body: The very first iPhone commercial was a compilation of clips from various TV shows and movies, featuring multiple characters answering the phone and saying "Hello." This advertising strategy aimed to highlight the device's fundamental communication capabilities. "Here is the first-ever iPhone commercial. It's better if you see it, but let me just say that it's a series of clips from various TV shows and movies. Hello. Hello. Hello."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: iPhone Introduction and Vision (2007)
podcast.body: On January 9th, 2007, Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone at MacWorld, articulating a vision for a revolutionary product that integrated three distinct devices: a wide-screen iPod with touch controls, a revolutionary mobile phone, and a breakthrough internet communications device. Jobs emphasized that these were not separate entities but "one device," signaling Apple's ambition to "reinvent the phone." "On January 9th, 2007, when Steve Jobs stepped onto the stage at an event called MacWorld. ... 'Well, today we're introducing three revolutionary products of this class. The first one is a wide-screen iPod with touch controls. The second is a revolutionary moldy thing. The third is a breakthrough internet communications device. ... An iPod, a phone, and an internet communicator, an iPod, a phone. Are you getting it? These are not three separate devices. This is one device. And we are calling it iPhone. Today, Apple is going to reinvent the phone.'"

podcast.title: Songs of Innocence Distribution (2014)
podcast.body: Apple facilitated the release of U2's *Songs of Innocence* to 500 million iTunes subscribers on September 9, 2014, as part of the iPhone 6 introduction. This "stunning technological feat" resulted in backlash from users who felt their personal music libraries were invaded. "The idea of distributing an album to 500 million people simultaneously is a stunning technological feat."

srcs.episode: Spectacular Acts of Self Sabotage

podcast.title: AAC File Format
podcast.body: Apple's proprietary file format, AAC (Advanced Audio Coding), was implemented for music available through the iTunes Music Store and for iTunes downloads. Despite the iPod's support for MP3s, Apple recognized the MP3's status as a de facto standard by including a feature in iTunes that allowed for the conversion of AAC files to MP3s. "Apple's proprietary file format was AAC, which stood for Advanced Audio Coding."

podcast.title: Acquisition of Sound Jam and iTunes Launch
podcast.body: In 2000, Apple acquired a product called Sound Jam, which was software designed for CD-ripping and MP3 playback, fulfilling Steve Jobs's ambition for the company to deeply engage with the music sector. This acquisition led to the software being renamed iTunes, which was then officially introduced on January 9, 2001. "So in 2000, the company bought a product called Sound Jam, which was CD-ripping and MP3 playback software."

podcast.title: Apple Lossless Audio Codec (ALAC)
podcast.body: Apple offers its own lossless audio codec, ALAC, as part of its commitment to delivering higher fidelity audio experiences. This initiative contributes to the growing market for high-resolution and lossless audio formats that aim to surpass the quality limitations of MP3s. "Apple has ALAC, Apple lossless audio codec."

podcast.title: Apple Music Spatial Audio
podcast.body: Subscribers to Apple Music have access to spatial audio, a premium feature designed to offer an immersive listening experience. This innovation reflects the ongoing evolution of audio technology and consumer demand for advanced sound quality beyond traditional compressed formats. "And if you have Apple music, there's spatial audio."

podcast.body: Apple operates Apple Music, which is currently the second-largest music streaming platform globally, behind Spotify. "Spotify is the biggest platform followed by Apple Music, and in third place, Amazon, largely because people are streaming music that they're Alexa Smart speakers."

podcast.title: Apple's Shift to Portable Music
podcast.body: Around the year 2000, Steve Jobs, after returning to a struggling Apple Computers, made a strategic decision to focus on portable music players, as he considered all existing options to be inadequate. This pivot laid the groundwork for the development of the iPod. "It was also around this time that Steve Jobs, who had arrived back at the struggling Apple computers, became focused on portable music players. He considered all of them awful."

podcast.title: Graphical User Interface Pioneer
podcast.body: Apple was recognized in the early 1990s for having a graphical user interface (GUI) for its machines, which other companies like Microsoft and IBM sought to surpass. Apple's pioneering work in GUIs set a benchmark for user-friendly computing that was aspired to by competitors. "That meant a graphical user interface that was hopefully better than what Apple had for their machines."

podcast.body: During the COVID-19 lockdowns, when people were confined to their homes, Apple Music experienced a significant surge in user engagement as individuals increasingly turned to streaming services for entertainment and connection. "Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube saw big spikes in users."

podcast.title: iPhone Cannibalization of iPod Sales
podcast.body: The extraordinary success of the iPhone led to an almost complete "cannibalization" of iPod sales. Consequently, Apple discontinued the iPod Nano and iPod Shuffle in the summer of 2017. The iPod Touch remains the sole available model, though its price point is now comparable to that of a low-end iPhone. "The bad news, if you want to call up that, is that the iPhone almost completely cannibalized. iPod sales. Apple stopped making the nano and the shuffle in the summer of 2017. But if you must have an iPod, you can still get one. But the only model available is the touch. And it really isn't that much cheaper than a brand new low-end iPhone."

podcast.title: iPhone Engineer Anxieties during Launch
podcast.body: During Steve Jobs's presentation of the iPhone, the engineers involved in the project reportedly harbored significant anxiety about whether the prototype on stage would function flawlessly as demonstrated. They consumed vodka shots, hoping the live demo would not crash. "Funny story, though. When Steve Jobs was making that presentation, the engineers working on that project weren't entirely confident that the phone their boss had on stage would work as promised. They sat there slugging back shots of vodka, hoping that the demo wouldn't crash and burn."

podcast.title: iPhone Sales and Company Transformation
podcast.body: The first iPhone went on sale on June 29th, 2007. Across all its generations, the iPhone has sold over 2.5 billion units, a phenomenon that transformed Apple from primarily a computer company into a dominant phone company and contributed to its valuation exceeding $2 trillion. "The first iPhone went on sale on June 29th, 2007. And through all the generations, it has sold somewhere north of 2.5 billion units. It turns Apple from a computer company into a phone company. And like I said earlier, a company worth $2 trillion."

podcast.title: iPod Commercials and Marketing Success
podcast.body: A key contributor to the iPod's monumental success was its "fantastically effective" television commercials. These advertisements famously featured dancing silhouettes highlighted by the device's distinctive white headphone cords, synchronized to popular music of the era. "A big part of that success had to do with a fantastically effective TV commercials for iPods with the dancing silhouettes highlighting the white headphone cords while the coolest music of the day played."

podcast.title: iPod Design Inspiration
podcast.body: The aesthetic design of the iPod was influenced by a 1958 transistor radio produced by Braun, while its control layout drew inspiration from a phone manufactured by the Danish company Bang and Olufsen. "The appearance was inspired by a 1958 transistor radio made by Braun, while the controls closely resembled a phone made by the Danish manufacturer Bang and Olivesson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: iPod Naming Origin
podcast.body: The name "iPod" was conceived by Vetti Chico, a freelance copywriter hired by Apple for the device's marketing. Inspired by the movie "2001: A Space Odyssey," Chico noted the player's resemblance to the white 'pods' used by astronauts and its function as a device that could connect to, yet operate independently from, a computer. "Vinnie was a fan of the movie 2001 Space Odyssey, and he thought that the all-white player looked a lot like the pods used by the astronauts of the spaceship Discovery for work outside the spacecraft. Another thing struck Vinnie. The new device was something that could be connected to and then operate independent from a computer, just like 2001's pods. And so it came to pass that this new device was christened the iPod."

podcast.title: iPod Project Codename and External Development
podcast.body: The internal codename for Apple's MP3 player project was P86. A significant portion of the development and engineering work was performed outside of Apple, leveraging a variety of external suppliers and partners. "The project to build an Apple-branded MP3 player was codenamed the P86. Most of the work was done outside Apple using a variety of suppliers."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: iPod Sales and Revenue Impact
podcast.body: The iPod achieved unprecedented success, becoming the fastest-selling portable music device of all time and a pivotal product that propelled Apple towards becoming a $2 trillion company. Apple sold 350 million iPod units in one-third of the time it took Sony to sell the same number of Walkmans. By 2006, iPod sales alone contributed 48% of Apple's total revenue. "The iPod became the fastest selling portable music device of all time and was the product that launched Apple on its way to becoming a $2 trillion company. Apple sold 350 million units in a third of the time. It took Sony to sell that many Walkmans. In 2006, iPod sales made up 48% of all of Apple's revenue."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: iPod Touch Market Niche
podcast.body: Despite the iPhone's prevalence, the iPod Touch, essentially an iPhone without cellular capabilities, maintains a market, particularly appealing to children. Over 100 million iPod Touches have been sold, accounting for approximately a quarter of all iPods ever sold. "But people still have used for what's basically an iPhone without the phone. For kids, for example, more than 100 million touches have been sold, which is about a quarter of all the iPods ever sold."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: iPod Trademark Disputes
podcast.body: Apple encountered several legal challenges regarding the "iPod" name. Joseph Grasso, an inventor from New Jersey, had previously trademarked the name years earlier and required financial compensation, a matter that took approximately four years to resolve. Additionally, an office furniture company in Michigan had been using the name "iPod" since 1991, and various other patent disputes also took years to settle. "But then there was the matter of Joseph Grasso, a New Jersey inventor who would come up with that name iPod a few years earlier and trademarked it. He needed to be compensated, which took about four years to sort out, by the way. And then there was an office furniture company in Michigan which used that name iPod as far back as 1991, or office furniture. That was sorted out. And there were a few other patent disputes of which took years to clear up."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: iTunes Music Store DRM
podcast.body: In its initial phase, music purchased from the iTunes Music Store incorporated digital rights management (DRM) tools. Apple's proprietary file format for these purchases was AAC (Advanced Audio Coding), although the iPod simultaneously supported other formats, including MP3s. "If you bought music from the iTunes Music Store, it did have digital rights management tools, at least at the beginning."

podcast.title: iTunes Music Store Dominance
podcast.body: Recognizing the music industry's struggle with illegal digital file sharing, Steve Jobs introduced the iTunes Music Store as a legitimate digital download option. It quickly became the dominant platform, controlling 70% of the worldwide market for legitimate digital music downloads, providing a crucial revenue stream for the struggling record labels in the face of cratering CD sales. "His iTunes music store, and it wasn't long before iTunes controlled 70% of the worldwide market for legitimate digital downloads."
